title: Matching Receipts
story: You paid for everything on a trip with a friend. Back home, your friend sends money for exactly two of your receipts, with only the total: target.
You have the receipt amounts in the order you paid them. Find the two receipts your friend paid for.
task: Write findPair(amounts, target). Return the positions (indexes) of the two receipts whose amounts add up to target, in either order.
Each receipt can be used once. There is always exactly one correct pair.
constraints: Exactly one pair of different positions adds up to target.

examples.explanation: 25 + 75 = 100, at positions 1 and 2. No other pair works: 40 would need a 60, and 15 an 85.
Two receipts can share an amount. 5 + 5 = 10, using positions 0 and 1. Using position 0 twice would not count.

hints: Pick one receipt, say the 25 in the first example. If it is part of the answer, what must the other amount be?
For each receipt a, the partner must be exactly target - a. So at every receipt, ask whether you have already seen target - a and at which position.
Which data structure answers "have I seen this value, and at what position?" in one step, without rescanning the list?

Walk the list once, keeping a hash map from amount to position. At each receipt, look up target - a first; if it is there, you are done. If not, store a with its position. Looking up before storing stops a receipt pairing with itself.
bruteForce: Try every pair: for each position i, check every later j for amounts[i] + amounts[j] === target.
It is correct, but pairs grow with n²: 10,000 receipts make about 50 million. The slow part is the inner loop searching the whole list for a partner every time.

walkthrough: The brute force searches for a partner from scratch for every receipt. Instead, remember what you have passed, so finding a partner is one lookup.
• At position 0 the amount is 40, so the partner would be 60. The map does not have 60, so store 40 → 0.
• At position 1 the amount is 25, so the partner would be 75. The map does not have 75, so store 25 → 1.
• At position 2 the amount is 75, so the partner would be 25. The map has 25 → 1, so return [1, 2].
Look up first, then store. If you stored first, a receipt of 50 with target 100 would find itself.
solution.timeWhy: One pass over the list, and each hash map lookup or insert is O(1) on average.
solution.spaceWhy: In the worst case the map holds every amount before the pair is found.
solution.takeaway: To find a partner for each element, store what you have seen in a hash map and look up the partner directly. This uses O(n) extra memory and removes the inner loop.
